sourceFile: IELTS Listening Mock Test 1 - Final Trimmed Version + Narrator Track

TEST01.title: MOCK TEST 1 (Final Trimmed Edition, with Narrator)

section1.script:
Test1_Sec0_Opening_Voice.mp3
NARRATOR: [clear, calm, announcer] This is IELTS Listening Mock Test One. You will hear four sections. You will have time to read the questions before each part begins. You should answer the questions as you listen. At the end of the test, you will have time to check your answers. Now, turn to Section One.
Test1_Sec1_Intro_Voice.mp3
NARRATOR: [clear, guiding] Section One. You will hear a conversation between a man who has recently moved to the area and a community arts coordinator. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 5.
NARRATOR: [clear, steady] Now listen and answer Questions 1 to 5.
Test1_Sec1_Part1_Voice.mp3
Emma: [warm, welcoming] Good morning, Riverside Community Arts Centre. Emma speaking. How can I help?
Daniel: [friendly, a little tentative] Hi, Emma. I've just moved into the area, and I'm interested in joining one of your evening classes.
Emma: [helpful, curious] Certainly. Are you looking for something creative?
Daniel: [thoughtful] Yes. I've done a little photography, mostly while travelling, but I've never had any formal training.
Emma: [encouraging] Our beginner photography group could be ideal. We cover composition, exposure and basic lighting.
Daniel: [pleased, curious] That sounds good. When does it meet?
Emma: [clear, matter-of-fact] Wednesday evenings.
Daniel: [confirming, hopeful] Wednesday works. What time does it start?
Emma: [clear, precise] At six thirty, and it finishes at eight fifteen.
Daniel: [curious] And how long does the course run?
Emma: [clear] Six consecutive weeks.
Daniel: [acknowledging] Okay.
Emma: [informative, descriptive] Most sessions are indoors, although there are two outdoor sessions. One is around the riverfront, focusing on reflections and low-light photography, and the other is in the old market district.
Daniel: [pleased] That's good. I was hoping there'd be some practical work.
Emma: [reassuring, informative] There certainly will be. The group has twelve places, and eight people have registered so far.
Daniel: [curious] And what's the fee?
Emma: [clear, matter-of-fact] Eighty-four pounds for all six sessions.
Daniel: [surprised] Eighty-four?
Emma: [confirming, reassuring] Yes, £84. That includes the photography handbook.
Daniel: [accepting] Fine.
Emma: [reassuring, warm] You don't need a professional camera. A smartphone is perfectly acceptable for the first two classes. You can bring a digital camera later if you have one.
Daniel: [pleased] I've got an old digital camera, so I'll probably use that later.
Emma: [warm] That's fine.
Daniel: [decisive, pleased] I'd like to register.
Emma: [warm, satisfied] Great.
Test1_Sec1_Transition_Voice.mp3
NARRATOR: [clear, guiding] Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 6 to 10.
30 SECONDS OF SILENCE (production marker — do not generate audio)
NARRATOR: [clear, steady] Now listen and answer Questions 6 to 10.
Test1_Sec1_Part2_Voice.mp3
Emma: [brisk, businesslike] Right, Daniel. Let's complete your registration. First, you'll need some identification.
Daniel: [curious] Would a driving licence be acceptable?
Emma: [clear, reassuring] Yes, that's fine. A passport is also acceptable, but the driving licence will do.
Daniel: [decisive] I'll bring that.
Emma: [matter-of-fact] We also need your postcode.
Daniel: [clear] It's SW18 4QJ.
Emma: [careful, confirming] S-W-18, 4-Q-J?
Daniel: [confirming] That's right.
Emma: [informative] Good. There's also a compulsory equipment charge of twelve pounds.
Daniel: [curious] What's that for?
Emma: [clear, informative] It covers the tripods and lighting equipment used during the indoor sessions.
Daniel: [calculating] So £84 plus £12?
Emma: [confirming, reassuring] Exactly. You don't need to buy any equipment yourself.
Daniel: [relieved] Good.
Emma: [clear, informative] The course begins on Wednesday the 14th of October.
Daniel: [confirming] The 14th. I'll put that in my calendar.
Emma: [helpful, informative] Please arrive about ten minutes early on the first evening. We'll issue you a temporary centre pass.
Daniel: [content] Fine.
Emma: [apologetic, clear] If you miss a class, we can't normally offer a refund because the fee covers the complete programme.
Daniel: [accepting] Okay.
Emma: [helpful, reassuring] However, classroom lessons are recorded and available through the online members' portal.
Daniel: [pleased] That's useful.
Emma: [warm, concluding] I'll email your registration confirmation later today.
Daniel: [grateful] Thanks very much.
Emma: [warm, closing] You're welcome.
Test1_Sec1_End_Voice.mp3
NARRATOR: [calm, concluding] That is the end of Section One. Now turn to Section Two.

section2.script:
Test1_Sec2_Intro_Voice.mp3
NARRATOR: [clear, guiding] Section Two. You will hear a museum guide giving visitors an orientation to the Riverside Heritage Museum. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 15.
NARRATOR: [clear, steady] Now listen and answer Questions 11 to 15.
Test1_Sec2_Part1_Voice.mp3
Claire: [warm, welcoming] Welcome to the Riverside Heritage Museum.
Claire: [friendly, inviting] I'm Claire, and I'll give you a brief orientation.
Claire: [informative] The museum occupies a converted nineteenth-century warehouse.
Claire: [informative] It originally stored goods arriving by river.
Claire: [clear, guiding] The main entrance is at the southern end of the building, facing Riverside Road.
Claire: [clear, guiding] On your floor plan, it's at the bottom.
Claire: [clear, steady] Immediately inside is the reception desk.
Claire: [clear, matter-of-fact] The Gift Shop is on the left of the entrance hall, and the toilets are on the right.
Claire: [confident, presenting] Straight ahead is the Main Exhibition Hall, which contains most of our permanent collection.
Claire: [informative, proud] The collection focuses mainly on the history of the river district, including trade and manufacturing.
Claire: [informative, reflective] The museum has expanded over the years, adding several smaller rooms around the original hall.
Claire: [informative, gentle] There's also a courtyard at the northern end, which is sometimes used for demonstrations and school activities.
Claire: [informative, cautionary] The archive is used by researchers, although ordinary visitors can't normally enter it.
Claire: [confident, transitional] I'll now explain the locations of the rooms marked A to I.
Test1_Sec2_Transition_Voice.mp3
NARRATOR: [clear, guiding] Before you hear the second part, you have some time to look at Questions 16 to 20. Look at the floor plan and identify the locations marked A to I.
30 SECONDS OF SILENCE (production marker — do not generate audio)
NARRATOR: [clear, steady] Now listen and answer Questions 16 to 20.
Test1_Sec2_Part2_Voice.mp3
Claire: [clear, guiding] Please look at the floor plan.
Claire: [clear, directional] We'll start at the main entrance at the bottom, facing north.
Claire: [clear, steady] The central corridor runs straight ahead.
Claire: [clear, confident] The first area on your immediate left, beside the Gift Shop, is A.
Claire: [matter-of-fact] That's the museum café.
Claire: [clear, guiding] Continue to the Main Exhibition Hall.
Claire: [clear, steady] On the left-hand side is B, the Temporary Exhibition Room.
Claire: [clear, confident] Directly opposite it, on the right, is C, the Local History Gallery.
Claire: [clear, guiding] Continue towards the northern end.
Claire: [clear, steady] Behind the Main Exhibition Hall, at the end of the corridor, is D, the Education Room.
Claire: [matter-of-fact] The small open area nearby is E, the courtyard.
Claire: [clear, guiding] Now return towards the entrance.
Claire: [clear, confident] On the right, just beyond the toilets, is F, the museum office.
Claire: [clear, confident] Immediately opposite it is G, the Photography Gallery.
Claire: [clear, guiding] Finally, look towards the eastern side of the Main Exhibition Hall.
Claire: [clear, confident] The River-View Gallery is H.
Claire: [clear, steady] Behind it is I, the Archive Room.
Claire: [cautionary, clear] Remember, the archive is not normally open to ordinary visitors.
Claire: [warm, delighted, closing] That's the end of the orientation.
Test1_Sec2_End_Voice.mp3
NARRATOR: [calm, concluding] That is the end of Section Two. Now turn to Section Three.

section3.script:
Test1_Sec3_Intro_Voice.mp3
NARRATOR: [clear, guiding] Section Three. You will hear a university research supervisor discussing a project about food-waste reduction with two students. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 25.
NARRATOR: [clear, steady] Now listen and answer Questions 21 to 25.
Test1_Sec3_Part1_Voice.mp3
Dr. Morris: [warm, welcoming] Good afternoon. I've read your revised proposal. Let's go through the main changes.
Dr. Morris: [curious, recalling] The original proposal focused on household food waste, didn't it?
Adam: [confident] Yes.
Sofia: [matter-of-fact] But household food waste has already been heavily researched.
Dr. Morris: [curious, probing] So why restaurants?
Sofia: [confident, explanatory] Restaurants can provide more measurable data because they keep purchasing and waste records.
Adam: [reflective, conceding] I initially preferred the household study, but the restaurant data should be more consistent.
Dr. Morris: [curious] What's your new research focus?
Adam: [confident, clear] Food-waste reduction practices in medium-sized restaurants, particularly how menu planning affects discarded food.
Dr. Morris: [precise, inquiring] How are you defining medium-sized?
Adam: [informative] We originally considered staff numbers.
Sofia: [explaining] But that's unreliable because many restaurants use part-time workers.
Dr. Morris: [curious] So?
Sofia: [clear, precise] Seating capacity. We're using restaurants with between forty and one hundred and twenty seats.
Dr. Morris: [approving, curious] Good. How will you collect the data?
Sofia: [thoughtful] We originally planned lengthy interviews with restaurant owners.
Adam: [explaining] But they were difficult to arrange during evening service.
Sofia: [confident, informative] So we've replaced those with analysis of weekly purchasing records and waste logs.
Adam: [informative] We'll also record changes to menus.
Dr. Morris: [cautionary] Remember that commercial records can be sensitive.
Adam: [reassuring] We've prepared a confidentiality agreement.
Dr. Morris: [approving, curious] Good. How many restaurants are you hoping to include?
Adam: [confident] Twenty-five originally.
Sofia: [realistic, measured] We've revised that to eighteen to twenty because that's more realistic.
Dr. Morris: [approving, curious] That's sensible. How many are interested?
Adam: [informative] Twelve so far.
Dr. Morris: [curious] And your main outcome measure?
Adam: [clear, explanatory] Percentage reduction in food waste, comparing average weekly waste before and after menu-planning changes.
Dr. Morris: [cautionary, instructive] Be careful about assuming the intervention caused every reduction. Customer numbers, seasonal effects, staffing and supply problems could also affect the results.
Sofia: [confident, reassuring] We've included those variables in the data sheet.
Dr. Morris: [pleased, curious] Excellent. And ethical approval?
Sofia: [informative] The initial paperwork has been submitted. We're waiting for the department's response.
Dr. Morris: [approving] Good.
Test1_Sec3_Transition_Voice.mp3
NARRATOR: [clear, guiding] Before you hear the second part of the discussion, you have some time to look at Questions 26 to 30.
30 SECONDS OF SILENCE (production marker — do not generate audio)
NARRATOR: [clear, steady] Now listen and answer Questions 26 to 30.
Test1_Sec3_Part2_Voice.mp3
Dr. Morris: [curious, organizing] Adam, what will you handle?
Adam: [confident] I'll analyse the purchasing records and calculate the percentage reduction in food waste.
Dr. Morris: [approving, instructive] Good. Keep the categories consistent across all restaurants.
Adam: [agreeing] I will.
Sofia: [engaged, confident] I'll conduct the interviews with kitchen managers.
Dr. Morris: [curious] Why kitchen managers?
Sofia: [explaining] They're directly involved in menu planning, portions and ingredient use.
Dr. Morris: [approving, instructive] Fine. Keep the interviews to around twenty minutes.
Sofia: [agreeing] We will.
Adam: [curious, proposing] What about the literature review? I thought we could divide it.
Sofia: [disagreeing, firm] I'd rather not. It needs to connect the quantitative and behavioural evidence.
Dr. Morris: [agreeing, instructive] I agree. You should write the literature review together.
Adam: [accepting] Okay.
Dr. Morris: [transitional] And the presentation?
Sofia: [confident] I'll design the slides.
Adam: [confident] I'll prepare the statistical graphs and explain the methodology.
Dr. Morris: [approving, gently teasing] Good. Keep the graphs simple.
Sofia: [curious] What about the conclusion?
Dr. Morris: [instructive, clear] Both of you should prepare it together. It needs to integrate the numerical findings and interview evidence.
Adam: [curious] And the recommendations?
Sofia: [confident] I'll present those.
Adam: [agreeing, confident] Then I'll take questions from the audience.
Dr. Morris: [approving] Good.
Dr. Morris: [curious] What about contacting the restaurants?
Adam: [confident] I can manage the data submissions.
Sofia: [agreeing] And I'll manage interview scheduling.
Dr. Morris: [pleased] That's a good division.
Dr. Morris: [instructive] Keep a contact log as well.
Adam: [agreeing] We'll do that.
Dr. Morris: [clear, concluding] So your immediate priorities are clear. Sofia, finalise the interview questions. Adam, finish the data spreadsheet. And both of you begin the literature review.
Sofia: [acknowledging] Understood.
Adam: [acknowledging] Okay.
Test1_Sec3_End_Voice.mp3
NARRATOR: [calm, concluding] That is the end of Section Three. Now turn to Section Four.

section4.script:
Test1_Sec4_Intro_Voice.mp3
NARRATOR: [clear, guiding] Section Four. You will hear a university lecturer talking about the science and environmental functions of urban wetlands. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.
NARRATOR: [clear, steady] Now listen and answer Questions 31 to 40.
Test1_Sec4_Full_Voice.mp3
Lecturer: [warm, engaging] Good afternoon.
Lecturer: [confident, informative] Today we're looking at urban wetlands and their role in managing environmental pressures in cities.
Lecturer: [clear, contrasting] Wetlands aren't necessarily remote marshes.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] They can exist beside rivers, around drainage channels, in city parks and on former industrial land.
Lecturer: [confident, organizing] I'll focus on four functions: stormwater management, water-quality improvement, biodiversity, and the challenge of combining ecological functions with public use.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Let's begin with stormwater.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Concrete and asphalt prevent water from soaking into the ground.
Lecturer: [clear, explanatory] In a natural landscape, some rainfall enters the soil, while vegetation absorbs and slows some of it.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Cities have large impermeable surfaces, so water moves rapidly towards drainage systems.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] When those systems become overwhelmed, flooding can occur.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, emphatic] An important point is that flood risk depends not only on how much rain falls, but also on how quickly water moves.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A wetland can temporarily store rainfall and release it more slowly.
Lecturer: [confident, explanatory] This reduces peak pressure on drainage infrastructure.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Wetlands don't eliminate floodwater, and their storage capacity is limited, so they should be part of a wider drainage system.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Now let's consider water quality.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Urban runoff can contain sediment, nutrients, oils and other pollutants.
Lecturer: [clear, explanatory] As water passes through dense vegetation, suspended particles can become trapped among plant roots and in wetland soils.
Lecturer: [informative, intrigued] Microorganisms in the sediments also contribute to treatment.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] One important example involves nitrogen.
Lecturer: [clear, explanatory] Nitrogen is necessary for plant growth, but excessive nitrogen entering rivers and lakes can cause eutrophication.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Eutrophication can stimulate excessive algae growth.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] When large quantities of algae die, microorganisms decompose them and consume oxygen.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] As oxygen levels fall, fish and other aquatic organisms may struggle to survive.
Lecturer: [clear, informative] Wetlands can help remove some nitrogen through microbial processes in waterlogged soils.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, cautionary] Their effectiveness depends on water movement, soil characteristics, temperature and vegetation.
Lecturer: [clear, cautionary] So simply constructing a pond does not automatically create an effective treatment wetland.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Let's move on to biodiversity.
Lecturer: [confident, warm] Urban wetlands can provide habitat for amphibians, insects, birds and aquatic plants.
Lecturer: [informative] For some species, a wetland provides a temporary refuge.
Lecturer: [informative] For others, it can become a breeding site.
Lecturer: [informative] Wetlands can also connect otherwise isolated green spaces.
Lecturer: [informative, intrigued] These connections can act as ecological corridors, allowing animals to move through urban areas.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, transitional] However, wetlands also attract people.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Residents may want walking routes, schools may want educational facilities, and visitors may want viewing platforms.
Lecturer: [balanced, measured] These activities can be compatible with conservation if access is carefully managed.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Heavy foot traffic can compact surrounding soil and affect water movement.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Visitors may also disturb nesting birds.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This is why wetlands often include boardwalks, viewing platforms and clearly defined routes.
Lecturer: [clear, informative] A raised boardwalk allows people to experience a wetland while reducing disturbance.
Lecturer: [confident, transitional] There is also an educational benefit.
Lecturer: [reflective] An underground drainage system is difficult for residents to understand.
Lecturer: [delighted, illustrative] A visible wetland allows people to see water being stored and managed.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, cautionary] However, wetlands can sometimes look untidy compared with conventional parks.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Mud, dead vegetation and changing water levels are normal ecological features.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Now let's return to engineering.
Lecturer: [clear, cautionary] Designing an effective urban wetland is not simply a matter of digging a pond.
Lecturer: [informative] Engineers need to consider water depth, seasonal rainfall patterns, soil composition and the surrounding drainage network.
Lecturer: [measured, emphatic] Water levels are particularly important.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] If a wetland remains permanently flooded, some plants may disappear.
Lecturer: [clear, explanatory] If it dries too frequently, its ability to retain water and support aquatic organisms may be reduced.
Lecturer: [clear, explanatory] Seasonal variation can therefore be beneficial.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Soil composition is also important.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Highly permeable soil may allow water to disappear too quickly, while impermeable soil can create other drainage problems.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, cautionary] Maintenance is another consideration.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Plants need monitoring, invasive species may need removal, and sediment can accumulate.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Drainage structures can become blocked, while boardwalks and viewing platforms require inspection.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, rhetorical] The important question is whether the wetland can continue performing its intended functions over many years.
Lecturer: [reflective, transitional] There is also a social dimension.
Lecturer: [confident, warm] Urban wetlands can provide recreational and educational spaces.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But excessive recreational use can damage vegetation, disturb wildlife and compact soil.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Successful projects therefore require managed access.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Why are urban wetlands becoming more important?
Lecturer: [measured, forward-looking] One reason is climate change.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] More intense rainfall events can place additional pressure on drainage infrastructure.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] At the same time, urban development reduces the amount of undeveloped land available for natural water storage.
Lecturer: [informative, impressed] A wetland can provide several functions at once: flood storage, water-quality improvement, wildlife habitat and recreation.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But wetlands are not a universal solution.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] They cannot eliminate flood risk or remove every pollutant, and they cannot completely replace conventional drainage infrastructure.
Lecturer: [clear, balanced] Instead, they can form part of a wider green-infrastructure strategy.
Lecturer: [informative] Green infrastructure includes rain gardens, green roofs, permeable surfaces and wetlands.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] The basic principle is to slow water down where possible.
Lecturer: [clear, explanatory] Rather than allowing rainfall to move immediately from roof to pipe to river, planners can create temporary storage areas.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, transitional] Another possibility is converting degraded urban land into wetlands.
Lecturer: [informative] Former industrial sites and unused drainage areas may sometimes be suitable.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] However, contaminated land creates additional challenges.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Engineers need to determine whether pollutants are present before construction begins.
Lecturer: [clear, informative] This is why urban wetland projects require collaboration.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Hydrologists study water movement.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Ecologists examine habitat and species.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Engineers deal with structures and drainage.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Urban planners consider land use.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Community specialists can help understand how residents will use the site.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, reflective] Success can also be measured in different ways.
Lecturer: [clear, illustrative] An engineer might examine whether flood pressure has been reduced.
Lecturer: [clear, illustrative] An ecologist might look at bird or amphibian populations.
Lecturer: [clear, illustrative] A water-quality scientist might measure nitrogen concentrations.
Lecturer: [warm, illustrative] Residents may simply ask whether the area has become a useful part of their neighbourhood.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] All these perspectives are relevant.
Lecturer: [measured, emphatic] So remember that an urban wetland is not simply a pond.
Lecturer: [confident, clear] It is a managed ecological system involving hydrology, soil, vegetation, microorganisms, wildlife and human behaviour.
Lecturer: [reflective, concluding] Modern planners increasingly view stormwater as something that can be temporarily stored, filtered and incorporated into the landscape.
Lecturer: [reflective, emphatic] That represents an important change in thinking.
Lecturer: [clear, illustrative] Instead of asking only how quickly water can be removed from a city, planners can ask where water can safely remain for a while.
Lecturer: [confident, warm] Cities need infrastructure that can respond to environmental pressures while providing ecological and social benefits.
Lecturer: [clear, concluding] Urban wetlands are one example.
Lecturer: [warm, forward-looking] Next week we'll examine green roofs and their contribution to urban climate adaptation.
Lecturer: [warm, concluding] Please read Chapter Nine before the seminar.
Test1_Sec4_End_Voice.mp3
NARRATOR: [calm, concluding, final] That is the end of the Listening test.
